name: Sara Moreau

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm head of science at Saltmarsh Academy, a secondary school in Port Elwyn, which is a fishing town at the end of a long coast road. My day is three or four lessons, a lot of Bunsen burners, and a free period where I'm fixing the fume cupboard or checking my team's lesson plans. I use AI every day, for planning, for quizzes, for rewriting worksheets for kids who read below their age. The best bit is a practical that works, when thirty fourteen-year-olds see copper turn green and gasp.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a rented house on Harbour Row with two friends, one's a vet nurse and one works at the fish market. My pay's on the lower end, because our trust is broke, so after rent and bills I've got maybe a fortnight's money in the bank at any time. There are only two secondary schools within fifty miles, so I'm here unless I want to leave the coast, and I don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a bit of a let-down, honestly, because I've got real gains from these tools. I'd tell other teachers the useful bits are still worth learning, like differentiating worksheets. Online I'd post a few of my favourite prompts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means I keep my job and keep being broke. AI saving me three hours a week is nice, but it doesn't change the fact that our trust pays the minimum and the rent on Harbour Row keeps climbing. The coast doesn't have spare jobs for a science teacher.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI to plan and adapt worksheets, and I'd run a staff session on it every term. I'd ask the trust for a small payment for running the training, since I do it for free now. And I'd pick up exam marking for the board in the summer for extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, mostly, with a bit of frustration. I'm not worried about my job in this picture. I'm worried about my bank balance, same as always.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How many hours a week does AI save you now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three, mainly on rewriting worksheets for kids with reading difficulties. That used to take me Sunday afternoons. Now I spend Sunday afternoons on the beach with a flask.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why haven't you asked for payment for the training before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I like doing it and I didn't want to seem greedy. But a vet nurse friend of mine pointed out I'm basically doing someone's job for free. She's right, and I'm skint.

say: I'd call it a **let-down**, since my AI tools give real gains.
I'd tell teachers the useful bits, like **adapting worksheets**, are still worth learning.
think: Privately, I'd keep my job and **keep being broke**.
Rent on Harbour Row keeps rising, and the coast has **few science jobs**.
do: Keep using AI to plan and **adapt worksheets** each week.
Ask the trust for **payment** for running staff AI training.
Pick up **exam marking** over the summer for extra money.
feel: Mostly fine, with some **frustration** about money.
S0.quote: AI saving me three hours a week is nice, but it doesn't change the fact that our trust pays the minimum and the rent on Harbour Row keeps climbing.
fieldNote: She is already a confident **daily user** and sees the plateau as a mild loss.
Her pressure is **low pay** and rising rent, not job security.
A friend prompted her to stop **training staff for free**, which she now plans to change.

steps.text: Run a termly staff session on AI for adapting worksheets
Ask the trust for a payment for running staff AI training
Keep teaching science at Saltmarsh Academy as before
Sign up to mark exams for the board each summer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's here, so let's make it work for kids and teachers, not for the companies selling it. I'd be pushing our union to bargain for AI that cuts workload without cutting jobs. Online I'd share what works and call out the rubbish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd do well out of this one, at least at first. I'm the person the trust already asks about AI, so I might get a trust-wide role. But I'd also watch them use it as an excuse not to replace teachers who leave, and that worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for any trust-wide digital lead role the moment it was advertised. I'd get the union to agree a rule that time saved by AI goes back to teachers, not into bigger classes. I'd also start an online course in data science for schools, because it fits what I already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and wary at the same time. I like change, but in my trust, money saved usually ends up as one less person.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at Saltmarsh?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our lab technician, Mr Pryce, who's been there thirty years. He orders chemicals, books equipment and keeps records, and software could do half of that. But the other half is hands-on, prepping practicals, and nobody else knows where anything is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd do well. What would the trust-wide role pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe two thousand pounds a year more, which for me is the difference between a fortnight's cushion and two months. A trust-wide role would also mean more travel up the coast road. I'd take it anyway.

say: I'd say make AI work for **kids and teachers**, not the companies selling it.
I'd push the union to bargain for **less workload**, not fewer jobs.
think: I might do well, perhaps landing a **trust-wide role**.
The trust could use AI as an excuse not to **replace teachers** who leave.
do: Apply for a **digital lead** role as soon as it's advertised.
Get the union to agree **time saved** goes back to teachers.
Start an online course in **data science** for schools.
feel: **Excited** and wary at the same time.
S1.quote: I like change, but in my trust, money saved usually ends up as one less person.
fieldNote: She expects to **gain** in this picture while worrying for colleagues.
She ties any new role to a concrete money goal: **two months** of cushion.
Her progressive view shows in insisting **time saved** goes to staff.

steps.text: Apply for the trust-wide digital lead role when advertised
Bargain through the union for AI time savings to go to teachers
Start an online course in data science for schools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this should belong to all of us, like the water or the roads. I'd be loud online about public ownership of AI and a guaranteed income. And at school I'd say we owe the kids honesty about what's coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my teaching job would shrink fast, because explaining and marking science is thinking work. The practicals give me maybe three extra years, until robots can handle a test tube. With a fortnight of savings, that's frightening, but I'm better placed than most because I know the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd offer myself to the trust to set up whatever AI system they bring in, because I'd rather design it than be replaced by it. I'd join the union campaign for a guaranteed income and retraining fund. And I'd move back to my mum's in the next town for a year if it meant saving rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, but also weirdly awake. I'd be one of the people who sees it first. That's a strange mix of dread and curiosity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your science classes that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my science classes that knowing how the world works still matters, even if a machine knows it too. Then I'd teach them to question what AI says, with real experiments. I'd want them to be the people who check, not the people who just believe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Moving back to your mum's. How would that feel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Embarrassing at twenty-seven, honestly. But Mum would love it and she has a spare room. I'd rather swallow my pride than be in debt.

I'd campaign for **public ownership** and a guaranteed income.
think: Explaining and marking science is **thinking work**, so my job would shrink fast.
**Practicals** give me roughly three extra years before robots catch up.
do: Offer to **set up** the trust's AI system rather than be replaced by it.
Join the union campaign for **guaranteed income** and retraining.
Move to **Mum's spare room** for a year to save rent.
feel: Scared yet **awake**, a mix of dread and curiosity.
S2.quote: I'd tell my science classes that knowing how the world works still matters, even if a machine knows it too.
fieldNote: She feels **better placed** than colleagues because she knows the tools.
She sees **lab practicals** as her short hands-on buffer.
Pride gives way quickly to **practical moves** like living with her mum.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up the trust's new AI system
Join the union campaign for a guaranteed income

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years to make this fair, so get organised. I'd be online and in the union, pushing for teachers to be trained and paid through it. I'd also say it's exciting, which some colleagues would hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years is enough for me to land on my feet. I'd be thirty-two, with good AI skills and a science degree. I'd worry more about my friends at the fish market than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the data science course in the first year and start building a portfolio of school AI projects. I'd take on paid AI training for other schools along the coast, maybe two days a term. And I'd save that money, every penny, into a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a knot underneath because I'm still broke. Five years gives me time to build something. It's not comfortable, but it's not panic either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your friends at the fish market. Why them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because their jobs are hands-on, but the buying and selling at the market is already going online. They'd get hit by the thinking AI first and the robots later. They've got less education than me and fewer options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave teaching altogether?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if something in AI for education paid properly. I'd miss the gasp when copper turns green. But I'm not sentimental about a job that pays me a fortnight's cushion.

I'd openly call it **exciting**, which some colleagues would hate.
think: Five years is enough for me to **land on my feet**.
I'd worry more for my **friends** at the fish market than myself.

Sell **AI training** to other coastal schools, two days a term.

fieldNote: Five years shifts her from survival to **building** a new path.

steps.text: Finish the data science for schools course this year
Sell AI training days to other schools along the coast
Put all training income into a separate savings account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case for planning properly as a country. I'd keep pushing for public AI, and for teachers to help design it. Online I'd be the optimist, which is a lonely place sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years suits me well. I'd be thirty-seven, probably working somewhere between a school and a tech team. The only thing that would really worry me is still having no savings by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching for a few years while building up my AI training work. I'd apply for a part-time secondment to the trust's digital team within two years. And I'd set up a standing order of a hundred pounds a month into savings, starting now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, honestly. I feel like I'd have a decent shot. The worry is more about money habits than robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A hundred pounds a month on your pay. Is that realistic?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if I get the training money or the trust role. On my teaching pay alone it would be fifty at best. I'd have to give up the takeaway coffee on the coast road, which I'd grieve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Saltmarsh Academy in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it survives, smaller, as a place for kids to be together and do real experiments. The teaching would be mixed, half AI and half us. I'd like to help shape what Saltmarsh Academy becomes, if they'd let me.

say: I'd say this is the best case for **planning properly** as a country.
I'd keep pushing for **public AI** with teachers helping design it.
think: Ten years **suits me**, with time to bridge school and tech.
My real worry is still having **no savings** by then.
do: Build AI training work while **teaching** for a few years.
Apply for a **secondment** to the trust's digital team within two years.
Set up a standing order of **£100 a month** into savings.
feel: Good, with a **decent shot** and some worry about money habits.
S4.quote: The teaching would be mixed, half AI and half us.
fieldNote: She is the most **optimistic** at ten years and sees a bridging role.
Her honest doubt is about **saving**, not technology.

steps.text: Keep teaching science while building outside AI training work
Apply for a part-time secondment to the trust's digital team
Set up a monthly standing order into a savings account

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because even I couldn't move fast enough with two weeks of savings. What would help is a public retraining fund and guaranteed income while it settles, so people like my friends at the market aren't left behind. And schools getting a say in which AI they use.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the kids think. My Year 10s already use AI for everything, and they're more scared than we are. They ask me if there'll be any jobs left, and I don't have a good answer yet.

headlineQuote: My Year 10s already use AI for everything, and they're more scared than we are.
portrait: Sara is a 27-year-old **head of science** at a secondary school in a coastal fishing town.
She uses AI **every day** and already trains other staff for free.
She shares a rented house and keeps only a **fortnight** of money in the bank.
She stays uneasy through the milder pictures and becomes **anxious** under AGI.
She would design the trust's AI and move to her mum's to **save rent** if needed.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because **two weeks** of savings leaves no room to move.
whatWouldHelp: A **public retraining fund** and guaranteed income while things settle.
Schools getting a **say** in which AI they use.
